items: The definition of “QS receptors” is too broad: counting generic two-component systems (TCS) as QS receptors risks substantial over-calling, since many TCSs sense environmental cues unrelated to QS.
Classifier features are limited to 20 amino-acid composition frequencies, which are unlikely to capture QS-specific signatures and are prone to learning taxonomic biases rather than function.
The term “ensemble classifiers” is used, but the work appears to train four separate models without a principled ensemble/consensus scheme or calibration.
Performance metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1) are referenced but not reported numerically; confusion matrices, ROC/PR curves, or calibration plots are missing.

Potential homology/annotation leakage: positives and negatives come from overlapping proteomes, and candidates are pre-filtered via BLASTP with a moderate E-value; a genus/species-held-out evaluation is not provided.
No benchmarking against strong domain-baseline methods (e.g., Pfam/InterPro HMMs for LuxI/LuxR, RpfF, PqsABCD/MvfR, LuxS/LsrB, AgrCA/peptides, ComDE/ComC).
Ambiguity in thresholds (e.g., “E value 105” likely means 1e−5), and “ensemble classifiers” terminology is confusing.
The mapping from predicted proteins to specific QS languages is insufficiently specified, particularly when labeling receptors to languages beyond canonical systems.
Limited discussion of domain/HMM-based QS detection and gene-cluster-level criteria that are commonly used for QS system identification.
No quantitative comparison against simple BLAST/HMM pipelines to isolate the incremental value of the ML classifiers.

The automated kcat “up-shifting” to the class maximum until growth matches an experimental target risks unrealistic kinetics and overfitting to growth rate, potentially biasing downstream predictions.

Exclusive reliance on Homo sapiens entries for ecHuman1 kcat assignment may be insufficient to populate tens of thousands of reactions; the feasibility and coverage of this choice need clearer justification and quantitative evidence.
The definition and handling of enzyme “saturation” metrics, particularly under constraint loosening or exclusion of incompatible proteomics entries, may confound interpretation of enzyme usage.

Limited benchmarking beyond growth-rate and gas-exchange metrics; little use of 13C fluxomics or independent enzyme activity/protein allocation datasets to validate internal predictions and claimed isoenzyme diversification effects.
The E. coli comparison uses a single ME-model and an SSE measure without detailed error normalization; broader baselines (e.g., MOMENT, RBA variants) and richer metrics would strengthen claims.
Lack of runtime and scalability characterization for the new FVA module and proteomics-integration workflow on the largest models (e.g., Human1).

Critical algorithmic details (phylogenetic distance measure, thresholds, unit conversion from specific activity to kcat, exact rules for loosening proteomics constraints) are deferred to supplementary materials and could be summarized more explicitly in the main text for reproducibility.
Calibration steps in the CI pipeline (e.g., how growth targets are applied, how re-calibration is handled upon upstream GEM changes) are not described with sufficient procedural detail.
While ME and RBA are discussed, there is limited quantitative comparison against other enzyme-capacity FBA variants (e.g., MOMENT, CAFBA, recent ecFBA pipelines).

The relationship to dynamic resource-allocation frameworks (e.g., dynamic eukaryotic RBA/dRBA) is not explored; the differences in data requirements, scope (steady-state vs dynamic), and trade-offs could be articulated to contextualize GECKO 2.0’s niche.

The dataset is very small (28 entries) relative to the chemical-design space, raising overfitting risk and limiting generalizability; 10-fold CV on n≈29 (including baseline) yields folds of size ~3 with potentially high variance.

The current feature representation treats a binary additive as a concentration-normalized sum of atomic descriptors, which may miss crucial higher-order interactions between functional groups and does not explicitly capture cross-additive synergies.

The decision to fix candidate dual-additive compositions to 1 wt% each during screening leaves composition optimization on the table; optimal loading and ratio are likely important and may be non-monotonic.
The reported MAEs for ASI and ΔASI (≈20 and ≈15 Ω·cm² on test folds) are large compared with the baseline and improvement margins, potentially blurring rank-ordering confidence.
Replicate counts, variability, and statistical significance of improvements are not reported; given known EIS and cycling variability, this is critical to support the claimed gains.
Grouped cross-validation (e.g., leave-one-additive-out or leave-one-scaffold-out) is not performed; sample-wise CV may leak additive identity across train/test and inflate apparent performance.
The final metrics (e.g., cycle number for “final” ASI, ΔASI, Q; formation and cycling protocols; temperature; EIS fitting procedure) are not fully specified in the main text.

Selection of the six validation candidates relies primarily on ΔASI and Q due to perceived model reliability, but a principled multi-objective/uncertainty-aware selection (e.g., Pareto fronts with expected hypervolume improvement) would better reflect trade-offs.
Table 1 contains clear errors: duplicated entry number “32” with radically different metrics; numbering inconsistencies (e.g., two “32” rows) undermine trust in reporting.

The “MS” acronym and structures appear inconsistent across text and Figure 2 (e.g., the figure transcription shows a LiFSI-like anion labeled “MS,” while the text describes “malonato tetrafluorophosphates”); this needs immediate clarification.
The Spearman correlation discussion sometimes reads inconsistently with the sign/direction in the plotted lists; clearer reconciliations and cautions about small-sample correlations are needed.

A statement that “SEM confirms the presence of TM aggregates in cells with additives, thereby reducing their detrimental effects” is confusing—why would aggregates reduce harm? This needs mechanistic clarification or rewording.

The paper cites relevant ML-for-electrolyte works but does not position its approach against recent closed-loop/robotic optimization and multi-objective discovery frameworks (e.g., Clio, ALBATROSS, Bayesian optimization in Otto/Dragonfly) in terms of methodology and throughput.
No benchmarking against alternative models (RF, SVR, XGBoost, multi-task GPs) or feature ablations is shown to justify GPR + the chosen descriptors as the best low-data choice.

Electrochemical window (ECW) estimation from gas-phase HOMO/LUMO levels is known to be unreliable and systematically overestimates oxidative stability; no solvation/condensed-phase corrections or explicit referencing to Li|Li+ are used.
Classification metrics are reported as “R²” for categorical tasks; appropriate metrics (accuracy, ROC-AUC, F1, precision/recall) and calibrated probabilities are missing.

Details of data curation and leakage control are insufficient: it is unclear whether IL-wise splits prevent the same IL (or same cation/anion family) from appearing in both train and test, which can inflate performance under sparse labels.
Inconsistencies and ambiguities in sample counts (e.g., 1240 vs 1084 liquids) raise questions about the exact training/labeling protocol and the temperature normalization for σ at RT.

tLi+ via Bruce–Vincent can be error-prone in concentrated IL/polymer systems; independent validation (e.g., eNMR, concentration-cell, or modern polarization-with-correction methods) would strengthen transport claims.

No quantification of Li content or ionic composition in the membranes (e.g., ICP-OES, elemental analysis, NMR), despite one IL failing to exchange Li; mechanistic claims about PBDT–ion interactions lack direct evidence.

Limited interphase diagnostics (e.g., XPS/TOF-SIMS of SEI/CEI, impedance evolution) to link stability to specific chemistries; mechanical properties (modulus, toughness, creep) of the membranes are not reported.

Hydrophilicity/processability constraints (aqueous casting) were applied post hoc during IL selection; these constraints are not part of the ML screen and thus reduce the end-to-end optimality of the pipeline.
Misrendered symbols (σ as “o”) and notational inconsistencies complicate interpretation; several equations lack unit/reference details.
GCN architecture and representation of cation–anion pairs (single combined graph? dual-graph fusion?) are not sufficiently specified to ensure reproducibility.
The rationale for the 5 mS cm⁻¹ threshold and its sensitivity analysis are not provided; ECW cutoff selection (3.5 V) is not justified against application-specific requirements.

No comparison against transfer-learning approaches that leverage COSMO-RS or MD pretraining to combat data sparsity (e.g., Sethi et al., 2509.10273), or recent multi-objective generative pipelines for electrolytes (e.g., conditional diffusion models).
Lack of ablations disentangling the value of Psi4 features versus purely topological/descriptor baselines, or of GCNs versus XGBoost under leakage-free splits.
No uncertainty quantification to guide experimental selection, despite the sparse/noisy label regime typical for ILs.

The LCE is trained on a relatively small set of 32 unique NEB hops; extrapolation across all local compositions may under-represent rare but rate-limiting local motifs or long-range electrostatics not captured in a local model.
Barriers are computed at 0 K on static lattices; vibrational free energy contributions, phonon-assisted effects, and temperature-dependent saddle-point softening are not explicitly included.
The framework focuses on bulk transport; grain-boundary, porosity, space-charge, and pellet/electrode contact effects that strongly affect EIS-derived conductivities are not modeled.
The assumption of random Si/P distributions based on high-T MC may not capture possible short-range ordering or synthesis-dependent polyanion clustering that can impact percolation.

Details on impedance analysis (bulk versus grain-boundary separation, electrode blocking behavior, fitting model and confidence intervals) are not fully elaborated; without this, quantitative comparison to bulk kMC predictions may be confounded by microstructural contributions.

The extent of experimental validation is limited to a subset of compositions; independent confirmation of predicted Haven ratios or tracer diffusivities via NMR/QENS would strengthen claims about correlated motion.

The kMC rate construction with KRA requires knowledge of endpoint energy differences to reconstruct directional barriers; it is unclear how site (Na(1)/Na(2)) energies were parameterized and whether a separate energetic CE was used.

Uncertainty quantification is limited: variance across polyanion configurations is partly shown (confidence band), but systematic error bars combining DFT barrier uncertainty, LCE fit errors, and kMC sampling noise are not fully propagated to σ and D.

The manuscript could better relate to contemporary strategies for barrier prediction and path enumeration (e.g., high-throughput NEB and ML-assisted NEB) and to multiscale treatments of grain-boundary effects in solid electrolytes, to position the present bulk-focused approach in the broader landscape.

A clearer discussion contrasting center-of-mass diffusivity–based conductivities with tracer-based measures and how these map to different experimental probes (EIS vs NMR/QENS) would help interpret Haven ratios and comparisons.
